punctuated:
學，制《為善隂隲》、《孝順事實》，弘敷彞倫之教，其大綱固無不正，萬目亦無不舉也。自是，仁宗昭皇帝、宣宗章皇帝、英宗睿皇帝，莫不繼體守成，益弘皇極之化，制禮作樂，大闡文明之治，其大綱固無不正，而萬目亦無不舉也。我列聖相承，能繼太祖高皇帝之治者，以其能心太祖高皇帝之心也。太祖高皇帝之心，即堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心也。
陛下嗣承大統，益弘至治，朝焉而惕，夕焉而厲，惓惓焉惟大綱之是正，業業焉惟萬目之是舉。臣有以知陛下是心，即堯、舜、禹、湯、文、武之心也，即祖宗列聖之心也。陛下即位之初，親幸辟雍，作興學校，嘗有意於明人倫、厚風俗矣，而人倫至今未甚明，風俗至今未甚厚；申飭有司，簡練將帥，嘗有意於安百姓、服夷狄矣，而百姓至今未甚安，夷狄至今未甚服，誠有如
translation_en:
…learning, and composed the Secret Merits of Doing Good (Weishan yinzhi) and the True Examples of Filial Piety (Xiaoshun shishi) to broadly propagate the teachings of invariant human relationships; thus the great foundational principles were certainly in no way incorrect, and the myriad details were likewise in no way left unaddressed. From that time on, Emperor Renzong the Illustrious, Emperor Xuanzong the Resplendent, and Emperor Yingzong the Wise all without exception succeeded to the line and conserved the achievements of their predecessors, further expanding the transformative influence of supreme perfection, instituting rites and creating music, and greatly unfolding a civil and enlightened governance; thus the great foundational principles were certainly in no way incorrect, and the myriad details were likewise in no way left unaddressed. That Our successive Sacred Emperors, inheriting one from another, were able to continue the governance of Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao was because they were able to take the mind of Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao as their own mind. The mind of Grand Progenitor Emperor Gao was none other than the mind of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu.

Your Majesty has succeeded to the Great Heritage and further expanded supreme governance, vigilant in the morning and tireless at night, earnestly intent only on rectifying the great foundational principles, and assiduously focused only on addressing the myriad details. Your servant thereby knows that this mind of Your Majesty is none other than the mind of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and none other than the mind of the Imperial Ancestors and successive Sacred Emperors. At the beginning of Your Majesty's reign, You personally visited the Imperial University (Piyong) and revitalized the schools; You indeed had the intention of clarifying human relationships and enriching popular customs, yet to this day human relationships are still not very clear, and popular customs are still not very rich. You issued strict orders to the authorities and selected and trained generals and commanders; You indeed had the intention of pacifying the common people and subjugating theforeign tribes, yet to this day the common people are still not very peaceful, and the foreign tribes are still not very submissive. It is truly just as…

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
陛下之所慮也雖然人倫之不明風俗之不厚百姓之未
富庶夷狄之未賓服其情狀之可矜事勢之不容已
雖族誅剡藤禿盡楚穎有未可勝言者臣愚不敢毛
舉其事溷
陛下之聽臣所知者其本在
陛下之一心也
陛下以天縱聰明之資首出庶物之德心無不正矣而臣
愚惓惓以是為言者臣之所學者在是帝王之致治
者在是
祖宗列聖之垂統者在是况人主之心攻之者衆或以貨
===
利或以聲色或以沉湎或以驕逸或以遊田或以奢
侈或以異端或以諂諛是數者一入而人主不能察
之則其心荒而大本不正矣大本不正雖欲正大綱
而大綱無自而正雖欲舉萬目而萬目無自而舉大
綱不正萬目不舉而欲望人倫之明風俗之厚百姓
之富庶夷狄之賓服是猶却步而求前倒植而求茂
也臣願
陛下謹之於幽獨得肆之地察之於虛明應物之時果天
理邪則敬以充之如火之始然使之燎于原如泉之
始達使之赴于海果人欲邪則敬以克之如火始然

punctuated: 陛下之所慮也。雖然，人倫之不明，風俗之不厚，百姓之未富庶，夷狄之未賓服，其情狀之可矜、事勢之不容已，雖族誅剡藤、禿盡楚穎，有未可勝言者。臣愚不敢毛舉其事，溷陛下之聽；臣所知者，其本在陛下之一心也。陛下以天縱聰明之資、首出庶物之德，心無不正矣；而臣愚惓惓以是為言者，臣之所學者在是，帝王之致治者在是，祖宗列聖之垂統者在是。况人主之心，攻之者衆：或以貨利，或以聲色，或以沉湎，或以驕逸，或以遊田，或以奢侈，或以異端，或以諂諛。是數者一入，而人主不能察之，則其心荒而大本不正矣。大本不正，雖欲正大綱，而大綱無自而正；雖欲舉萬目，而萬目無自而舉。大綱不正，萬目不舉，而欲望人倫之明、風俗之厚、百姓之富庶、夷狄之賓服，是猶却步而求前、倒植而求茂也。臣願陛下謹之於幽獨得肆之地，察之於虛明應物之時：果天理邪，則敬以充之，如火之始然，使之燎于原，如泉之始達，使之赴于海；果人欲邪，則敬以克之，如火始然
translation_en: …Your Majesty’s concerns. Even so, as for why human relationships are not clarified, customs are not generous, the common people are not yet prosperous and numerous, and the barbarian tribes have not yet submitted in allegiance—their pitiable conditions and the urgency of the circumstances could not be fully recounted even if one were to exterminate the whole clan of Shan-creek rattan for paper and wear bald every writing brush of Chu. In my foolishness, I dare not enumerate every trivial detail of these matters and trouble Your Majesty’s hearing; what I do know is that the root of it all lies in Your Majesty’s single mind. With Your Majesty’s heaven-bestowed intelligence and wisdom, and Your virtue that stands preeminent above all things, there is nothing in Your mind that is not rectified. Yet the reason I, in my foolishness, earnestly speak of this is that what I have studied lies herein, the way emperors and kings bring about good governance lies herein, and the heritage handed down by Your ancestors and the succession of sacred emperors lies herein. Moreover, those that assail the mind of a ruler of men are many: some through wealth and profit, some through music and women, some through drunken indulgence, some through arrogance and ease, some through pleasure excursions and hunting, some through extravagance, some through heterodox teachings, and some through flattery and sycophancy. Once any of these several things enters in and the ruler of men fails to discern it, his mind becomes neglected and the great foundation is not rectified. When the great foundation is not rectified, even though one wishes to rectify the mainstays, the mainstays have no means to be rectified; even though one wishes to raise up the myriad meshes of the net, the myriad meshes have no means to be raised. If the mainstays are not rectified and the myriad meshes are not raised, yet one hopes for human relationships to be clarified, customs to be generous, the common people to be prosperous and numerous, and the barbarian tribes to submit in allegiance, this is like walking backward while seeking to advance, or planting a tree upside down while seeking to make it flourish. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty be vigilant over Your mind in the solitary places where one might easily give rein to oneself, and examine it at the moments when, clear and unclouded, it responds to external things: if a thought is truly Heavenly Principle, then reverently expand it—like a fire just beginning to burn, cause it to blaze across the plain; like a spring just beginning to flow forth, cause it to rush to the sea. If it is truly human desire, then reverently overcome it—like a fire just beginning to burn…

…is immediately extinguished, not allowing it to gain the momentum to set the prairie ablaze; and like a spring just beginning to flow that is immediately dammed up, not allowing it to cause the disaster of an overflowing flood. Through this, Heavenly Principle will grow brighter day by day, human desires will melt away day by day, the mind will be entirely rectified, and the great foundation will be established. Once the great foundation is established, the great guiding principles will thereby be rectified and the myriad particulars will thereby be raised up. Once the great guiding principles are rectified and the myriad particulars are raised up, human moral relations will become clear of themselves without one's seeking their clarity; customs will become generous of themselves without one's seeking their generosity; the common people will become prosperous and numerous of themselves without one's seeking their prosperity and numbers; the foreign tribes will submit in allegiance of themselves without one's seeking their submission; and all manner of felicitous things and attainable auspicious omens will gather like clouds and gush forth like rivers. Through this you will add glory to the imperial ancestors, and through this you will match the splendor of the former emperors and kings. Governance today will be none other than the governance of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, and Wu, and none other than the governance of the successive sagely imperial ancestors.

Yet if one seeks the governance of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the successive sagely imperial ancestors, one must seek the mind of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the successive sagely imperial ancestors; and if one seeks the mind of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the successive sagely imperial ancestors, one must seek the learning of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the successive sagely imperial ancestors. The learning of Yao, Shun, Yu, Tang, Wen, Wu, and the successive sagely imperial ancestors is none other than the Way of the Great Learning (Daxue). The Way of the Great Learning has eight specific steps: bringing peace to all under Heaven, governing the state, regulating the family, cultivating the personal life, rectifying the mind, making the intentions sincere, extending knowledge, and investigating things. The essential point of bringing peace to all under Heaven, governing the state, and regulating the family lies in cultivating the personal life; the essential point of cultivating the personal life lies in rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere; and the essential point of rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere lies in extending knowledge and investigating things. The essentials of cultivating the personal life are two: being prudent in word and deed, and rectifying one's dignified demeanor. The essentials of rectifying the mind and making the intentions sincere are two: exalting reverent awe, and guarding against indulgent desires. As for exalting reverent awe: in serving Heaven and governing the people, it is this reverence; in cultivating oneself, it is this reverence; in encountering calamities, it is this reverence. As for guarding against indulgent desires: against wallowing in dissipation and arrogant idleness, it is this vigilance…

punctuated: 也，奢侈遊田此戒也。格物致知之要有三：明道術、審治體、辨人材是也。明其道術，則必察吾道源流之正、異端悖謬之失，辨王道純粹之誠、伯術駁雜之偽；辨人材，則必察姦雄竊國之柄、憸邪罔上之情；察民情，則必審民心向背之由、閭里戚休之實。從事乎此，日與公卿大臣、賢士大夫講明於萬幾之暇，致察於幽獨之中，不憚其難為，不忽其易為，則物無不格，知無不至，意無不誠，心無不正，身無不脩。舉是而措之於家，則家無不齊；舉是而措之於國，則國無不治；舉是而措之於天下，則天下無不平。唐、虞、三代之大綱無不正、萬目無不舉，用此道也；漢、唐、宋之或大綱正而萬目未舉，或萬目舉而大綱不正，不用此道也。祖宗之所以正大綱、舉萬目，而致唐、虞、三代之治，固用此道矣。陛下欲正大綱、舉萬目，而繼祖宗列聖之治，可不用此道乎？自唐、虞而三代，自三代而漢、唐、宋，用是道則治，不用是道則否；用是道則安，不用是道則危；用是道則長久，不用是道則短促。然則是道也，治道興衰之所係，國祚長短之所關，
translation_en:
…; extravagance, roaming, and hunting—against these one must guard. There are three essentials to investigating things and extending knowledge: clarifying the Way and its methods, examining the principles of governance, and distinguishing men of talent. To clarify the Way and its methods, one must examine the orthodoxy of the origin and transmission of our Way and the errors of the perverse fallacies of heterodox teachings, and distinguish the pure sincerity of the Kingly Way from the mixed falsehood of the Hegemon's techniques. To distinguish men of talent, one must examine how treacherous opportunists usurp the handles of the state and the circumstances in which crafty villains deceive their superiors. To examine the conditions of the people [note: corresponding to "examining the principles of governance" above], one must scrutinize the reasons why the people's hearts turn toward or away from the ruler, and the realities of sorrow and joy in the villages and lanes. Engaging in these pursuits, daily discussing and clarifying them with the dukes, ministers, high officials, and worthy scholar-officials during moments of leisure from the myriad affairs of state, and carrying out careful scrutiny in the solitude of one's own privacy—neither shrinking from what is difficult to do nor neglecting what is easy to do—then there will be no thing uninvestigated, no knowledge unextended, no thought insincere, no mind unrectified, and no person uncultivated. Take this and apply it to the family, and no family will not be regulated; take this and apply it to the state, and no state will not be rightly governed; take this and apply it to All under Heaven, and All under Heaven will not fail to be brought to peace.

That under Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties the great guiding principles were never unrectified and the myriad details were never unaddressed was because they employed this Way. That under the Han, Tang, and Song either the great guiding principles were rectified while the myriad details were left unaddressed, or the myriad details were addressed while the great guiding principles were unrectified, was because they did not employ this Way. The means by which the Imperial Ancestors rectified the great guiding principles, addressed the myriad details, and achieved the governance of Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties was assuredly by employing this Way. If Your Majesty wishes to rectify the great guiding principles, address the myriad details, and continue the governance of the Imperial Ancestors and the successive sage emperors, how could you not employ this Way? From Tang and Yu to the Three Dynasties, and from the Three Dynasties to the Han, Tang, and Song, when this Way was employed there was order, and when this Way was not employed there was disorder; when this Way was employed there was security, and when this Way was not employed there was danger; when this Way was employed the dynasty endured for a long time, and when this Way was not employed it was cut short. This being so, upon this Way depends the rise and decline of good governance, and with it is bound up the longevity or brevity of the dynasty's reign; …

translation_en: … can Your Majesty not take some warning to heart? The Book of Changes (Yi) says: "Rectify one's heart, and the myriad affairs will be in order; an error of a hair's breadth leads to a discrepancy of a thousand li." Master Zeng (Zengzi) said: "Revere what one has heard, and one becomes lofty and great; practice what one knows, and one becomes illustrious and bright." Being lofty, bright, illustrious, and great lies in nothing else, but solely in applying one's mind to it. What your servant has set forth I certainly dare not make overly broad, nor dare I make overly brief; gathering the words of grass-cutters and firewood-gatherers, I presumptuously impose upon Your Heavenly Hearing, wishing only that Your Majesty might deign to cast Your imperial gaze upon them and likewise apply Your mind to them. Overcome with fear and trembling, your servant respectfully replies.

臣對：臣聞《中庸》曰：「凡為天下國家有九經，所以行之者一也。」盖一者，誠也。以之脩身，則有以正天下之大□；以之□治，則有以舉天下之萬目。大哉誠乎！亘萬古而不息，放四海而皆準。人倫由是而明，風俗由是而厚，蒼生由是而富庶，四夷由是而咸賓。堯、舜以之而帝，三王以之而王。我朝太祖以之創業，列聖以之守成，陛下所以增光於祖宗、匹休於往聖，亦惟本於此誠而已。自漢徂唐，由唐迨宋，綱正矣而目則未舉者，無是誠以本之也；目舉矣而綱則未正者，無是誠以基之也。欽惟皇帝陛下誕膺駿命，茂纘丕圖，賤貨貴德，一此誠而不雜；制治保邦，守此誠而不踰。內而聖母太后日夕化導之切，外而執政大臣左右輔弼之勤，所以登三而邁五、光前而裕後者，端有在於此矣。伏
translation_en:
Your servant Cheng Minzheng 程敏政.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that the Doctrine of the Mean (Zhongyong) says: "In all governing of the empire and the state there are nine standard rules, and the means by which they are practiced is one." Now, that "one" is sincerity. When one uses it to cultivate the self, one has the means to rectify the great [headrope/fundamental?] of the empire; when one uses it to [effect?] governance, one has the means to raise up the ten thousand meshes of the empire. Great indeed is sincerity! It spans ten thousand ages without ceasing, and when extended to the four seas it is everywhere the standard. Human moral relations are thereby made clear; customs are thereby made generous; the common people are thereby made prosperous and numerous; the four barbarian peoples are thereby all brought to submission as guests. Yao 堯 and Shun 舜 used it to rule as emperors; the Three Kings used it to rule as kings. In our dynasty, the Grand Progenitor (Taizu 太祖) used it to found the imperial enterprise, and the successive sacred emperors used it to preserve the accomplishment. That by which Your Majesty adds luster to the ancestors and matches the splendor of the former sages is likewise rooted solely in this sincerity and nothing more. From the Han to the Tang, and from the Tang down to the Song, where the headrope was rectified yet the meshes were not raised up, it was because they lacked this sincerity as their root; where the meshes were raised up yet the headrope was not rectified, it was because they lacked this sincerity as their foundation. Your servant reverently reflects that Your Imperial Majesty has grandly received the great mandate and flourishingly succeeded to the vast plan. Scorning wealth and prizing virtue, You unify this sincerity without admixture; regulating governance and securing the state, You guard this sincerity without transgression. Within the palace, there is the earnest transforming guidance of the Sacred Mother, the Empress Dowager, morning and evening; in the outer court, there is the diligent assistance of the grand ministers holding the reins of government at Your left and right. That by which You ascend to the level of the Three Kings and surpass the Five Emperors, glorifying predecessors and enriching posterity, truly lies right here. Humbly…

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
猶體道謙沖不自滿假首進臣等于
廷詢以治道所謂智出天下而聽於至愚威加四海而
屈於匹夫臣知
陛下可以堯舜可以湯武可與措刑而富國可與强兵而
伏戎矣然切思之開茂科策多士
祖宗以来相承既久未知今日
陛下之意姑以遵
累朝之舊典備他日之故事而已耶抑真欲周詢衆論
博盡群言以冀萬分之一助也臣誠愚昧不知所出然
究心於正學留意於時政亦有年矣今獲登
===
大廷奉清問敢不精白一心傾竭底蘊以答
淵衷塞
明詔臣聞治天下有本焉大綱是也有末焉萬目是也
大綱不正則治道有未純萬目不舉則治法有未備
然大綱之或正或否萬目之或舉或遺則係於人君
此心之誠何如耳臣嘗觀於唐虞之際欽明文思而
允執厥中堯之德一於誠也濬哲文明而允迪厥德
舜之德一於誠也是以惇叙九族藹然公族之親釐
降二女肅然閨門之禮內承頑父秉夔夔之誠外撫
傲弟盡烝烝之乂尚何大綱之不正哉内有百揆四

降二女肅然閨門之禮內承頑父彔嚚之誠外協
傲弟盡烝烝之乂尚何大綱之不正哉內有百揆四
punctuated:
猶體道謙沖，不自滿假，首進臣等于廷，詢以治道。所謂智出天下而聽於至愚，威加四海而屈於匹夫，臣知陛下可以堯舜，可以湯武，可與措刑而富國，可與强兵而伏戎矣。然切思之，開茂科，策多士，祖宗以来，相承既久，未知今日陛下之意，姑以遵累朝之舊典，備他日之故事而已耶？抑真欲周詢衆論，博盡群言，以冀萬分之一助也？臣誠愚昧，不知所出，然究心於正學，留意於時政，亦有年矣。今獲登大廷，奉清問，敢不精白一心，傾竭底蘊，以答淵衷，塞明詔？

臣聞治天下有本焉，大綱是也；有末焉，萬目是也。大綱不正，則治道有未純；萬目不舉，則治法有未備。然大綱之或正或否，萬目之或舉或遺，則係於人君此心之誠何如耳。臣嘗觀於唐虞之際，欽明文思而允執厥中，堯之德一於誠也；濬哲文明而允迪厥德，舜之德一於誠也。是以惇叙九族，藹然公族之親；釐降二女，肅然閨門之禮；內承頑父，秉夔夔之誠；外撫傲弟，盡烝烝之乂，尚何大綱之不正哉？内有百揆四…
translation_en:
…yet You still embody the Way with modest humility and do not rest in self-satisfaction, first summoning Your servants to the court to inquire about the way of governance. This is what is meant by having wisdom that surpasses the world yet listening to the most foolish, and majesty that extends across the Four Seas yet bowing before a commoner. Your servant knows that Your Majesty can become like Yao and Shun, can become like Tang and Wu, and is one with whom penalties can be set aside and the state enriched, with whom the army can be strengthened and the western barbarians subdued. Yet when I earnestly reflect upon it: opening this flourishing examination and putting policy questions to the multitude of scholars is a tradition handed down from the imperial ancestors for a long time now; I do not know whether Your Majesty's intention today is merely to follow the established canons of successive reigns and fulfill a formality for another day? Or do You truly wish to inquire broadly into public opinion and exhaustively gather the words of the many, in hopes of gaining even one ten-thousandth of a help? Your servant is truly foolish and ignorant, not knowing how to proceed; yet I have devoted my mind to orthodox learning and paid heed to current governance for some years now. Having today been permitted to ascend the great court and receive Your pure inquiry, how could I dare not keep a pure and single heart and pour out my innermost thoughts in full, so as to answer Your profound mind and fulfill Your luminous decree?

Your servant has heard that in governing the realm there is a root: this is the great headrope; and there are branches: these are the ten thousand meshes. If the great headrope is not rectified, the way of governance will not yet be pure; if the ten thousand meshes are not lifted, the methods of governance will not yet be complete. Yet whether the great headrope is rectified or not, and whether the ten thousand meshes are lifted or neglected, depends solely on the sincerity of the ruler's own mind. Your servant has observed the era of Tang and Yu: reverent, enlightened, accomplished, and thoughtful, and sincerely holding fast the Mean—the virtue of Yao was unified in sincerity; profoundly wise, civilized, and enlightened, and sincerely pursuing his virtue—the virtue of Shun was unified in sincerity. Therefore, in generously ordering the nine grades of kinsmen, there was the harmonious affection of the ruling clan; in sending down his two daughters in marriage, there was the solemn propriety of the inner quarters; within, serving an obstinate father, he maintained a reverently fearful sincerity; without, soothing an arrogant younger brother, he exhausted the governance of progressive improvement—what great headrope, then, was not rectified? Within, there were the General Regulator and the Four…

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
岳外有州牧侯伯命羲和以典曆象而敬天勤民之
政舉命夷夔以典禮樂而化民成俗之道明庶政以
之而咸熈府事以之而允治則萬目亦無有不舉者
矣臣嘗觀於三代之時惟日孜孜而大德之是懋禹
湯之誠也小心翼翼而細行之亦矜文武之誠也是
以彝倫攸叙而文命敷于四海人紀肇脩而帝命式
于九圍后妃有關雎窈窕之德公族有麟趾信厚之
風尚何大綱之不正哉有典則以貽子孫而鈞石之
度無不具制官刑以警有位而風愆之戒為甚嚴六
典八法之制無一之不備五禮六樂之法無一之不
===
周則萬目亦無有不舉者矣此二帝三王之治所以
正大綱舉萬目者無非本於誠也漢之高帝喪義帝
則君臣之義明尊太公則父子之倫正封同姓以連
城非私也所以惇周親祀孔子以太牢非過也所以
崇聖道其大綱之正良可美也然制禮頗襲於秦而
用之朝廷者乃綿蕞之儀作樂不稽於古而奏之郊
廟者乃趙代之謳定律令而八刑糾民之法墮申軍
法而九伐正邦之意泯建官無制而太尉御史位乃
參於三公養民無法而强宗閭右田或連夫阡陌是
以世代相承德化不純而萬目則未舉也其所以未

punctuated: 岳，外有州牧、侯伯；命羲、和以典曆象，而敬天勤民之政舉；命夷、夔以典禮樂，而化民成俗之道明。庶政以之而咸熈，府事以之而允治，則萬目亦無有不舉者矣。臣嘗觀於三代之時，惟日孜孜而大德之是懋，禹、湯之誠也；小心翼翼而細行之亦矜，文、武之誠也。是以彝倫攸叙，而文命敷于四海；人紀肇脩，而帝命式于九圍。后妃有《關雎》窈窕之德，公族有《麟趾》信厚之風，尚何大綱之不正哉？有典則以貽子孫，而鈞石之度無不具；制官刑以警有位，而風愆之戒為甚嚴。六典、八法之制無一之不備，五禮、六樂之法無一之不周，則萬目亦無有不舉者矣。此二帝、三王之治，所以正大綱、舉萬目者，無非本於誠也。漢之高帝，喪義帝則君臣之義明，尊太公則父子之倫正。封同姓以連城，非私也，所以惇周親；祀孔子以太牢，非過也，所以崇聖道。其大綱之正，良可美也。然制禮頗襲於秦，而用之朝廷者乃綿蕞之儀；作樂不稽於古，而奏之郊廟者乃趙、代之謳。定律令，而八刑糾民之法墮；申軍法，而九伐正邦之意泯。建官無制，而太尉、御史位乃參於三公；養民無法，而强宗、閭右田或連夫阡陌。是以世代相承，德化不純，而萬目則未舉也。其所以未
translation_en:
… the Four Mountains, and outside there were the Pastors of the Provinces and the Archer-Lords and Leaders. They commanded Xi and He to take charge of the calendar and astronomical phenomena, whereby the governance of revering Heaven and working diligently for the people was upheld; they commanded Yi and Kui to take charge of rites and music, whereby the Way of transforming the people and perfecting customs was made clear. Through this, all governmental affairs were universally prosperous, and the six treasuries and three businesses were truly well-ordered; thus, among the myriad details, there was none that was not upheld.

Your servant has also observed the era of the Three Dynasties: thinking tirelessly day by day and exerting themselves in great virtue—such was the sincerity of Yu and Tang; being reverently cautious and taking care even in minor conduct—such was the sincerity of King Wen and King Wu. Therefore, the constant human relationships were set in order, and cultural teachings spread throughout the Four Seas; the moral bonds of humanity were first cultivated, and the Sovereign's mandate served as a model throughout the Nine Divisions. The consorts possessed the modest and virtuous character celebrated in the "Guanju" ode, and the royal clan had the trustworthy and generous customs praised in the "Linzhi" ode—how then could the great overarching principles not be rectified? They possessed canons and rules to bequeath to their descendants, so that even the standard weights of the jun and shi were completely provided for; they instituted official punishments to warn those in office, making the admonitions against decadent faults extremely strict. Of the institutions of the Six Canons and Eight Laws, not one was incomplete; of the regulations of the Five Rites and Six Musics, not one was incomprehensive. Thus, among the myriad details, there was none that was not upheld. That by which the governance of these Two Emperors and Three Kings rectified the great overarching principles and upheld the myriad details was rooted entirely in sincerity.

As for Emperor Gao of the Han: when he mourned Emperor Yi, the righteousness between ruler and minister was made clear; when he honored the Grand Sire (Taigong), the moral relationship between father and son was rectified. His enfeoffing men of the same surname with contiguous cities was not out of private favor, but the means to foster close kin; his sacrificing to Confucius with the grand offering of all three livestock (tailao) was not excessive, but the means to revere the Way of the Sage. The rectitude of his great overarching principles is truly praiseworthy. Yet in establishing rites he largely inherited those of Qin, so that what was used in the imperial court was merely the makeshift ceremonial drafted with ropes and bundled grass (mianzui); in creating music he did not examine antiquity, so that what was performed at the suburban sacrifices and ancestral temples was merely the folksongs of Zhao and Dai. When he fixed the statutes and ordinances, the system of the Eight Punishments for correcting the people fell into ruin; when he proclaimed military law, the meaning of the Nine Campaigns for rectifying the states vanished. In establishing offices there was no proper system, so that the positions of Grand Commandant (taiwei) and Censor-in-Chief (yushi) were ranked alongside the Three Dukes (sangong); in nourishing the people there was no proper method, so that powerful clans and wealthy magnates of the neighborhoods had fields stretching across the grid of paths and ridges. Therefore, as generations succeeded one another, moral transformation remained impure, and the myriad details were not upheld. The reason they were not…

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
舉者誠有未至而雜於霸也唐之太宗定府兵之制
而農無養兵之費立世業之法而下無兼并之患以
租庸任民則農有定業以職事任官則官無虛名其
萬目之舉深可嘉也然脅父以起兵則君臣之義睽
迫父以傳位則父子之道缺蹀血宮門則兄弟之情
薄麀聚後庭則夫婦之倫亂以王姬之貴而下嫁夷
虜之酋是伉儷非偶也以天子之尊而下靺可汗之
號是華夷無別也是以子孫相繼慚德爲多而大綱
則未正也其所以未正者誠有未修而雜於夷也宋
祖開基仁義立國遵慈訓而不違金匱之盟可以見
===
其孝愛晋王而卒授神器之重可以見其友家法之
正而宮闈之醜未聞也傳授審明而迫奪之禍無有
也洞開諸門而悟君心之當正蓋有契乎正心之學
偶讀二典而嘆法網之太密蓋有得乎敬刑之旨然
宋之大綱固無愧於三代而宋之法制則不迨於漢
唐以詩賦記誦求士而無學校養成之法以科名資
歷叙位而無官司課試之方選宿衛則不能變五代
姑息羈縻之俗教宗室則無以合先王親疎隆殺之
宜國用常病於空虛兵威常患於不振萬目未盡舉
者亦以誠之有未至也漢宋大綱雖云正矣然因寵

其孝愛晉王而舉授神器之重可以見其友家法之
正而宮闈之醜未聞也傳授眾明而逼奪之禍無有
也洞開諸門而悟君心之當正蓋有契乎正心之學
偶讀二典而嘆法網之太密蓋有得乎敬刑之旨然
宗之大綱固無愧於三代而宋之法制則不追於漢

姑息驕縱之俗教宗室則無以合先王親疏隆殺之
宜國用常病於空虛兵威常患於不振萬目未盡舉
者亦以誠之有未至也漢宋大綱雖云正矣然因竊
punctuated: 舉者，誠有未至而雜於霸也。唐之太宗定府兵之制，而農無養兵之費；立世業之法，而下無兼并之患；以租庸任民，則農有定業；以職事任官，則官無虛名。其萬目之舉，深可嘉也。然脅父以起兵，則君臣之義睽；迫父以傳位，則父子之道缺；蹀血宮門，則兄弟之情薄；麀聚後庭，則夫婦之倫亂。以王姬之貴而下嫁夷虜之酋，是伉儷非偶也；以天子之尊而下靺可汗之號，是華夷無別也。是以子孫相繼，慚德爲多，而大綱則未正也。其所以未正者，誠有未修而雜於夷也。宋祖開基，仁義立國。遵慈訓而不違金匱之盟，可以見其孝；愛晋王而卒授神器之重，可以見其友。家法之正，而宮闈之醜未聞也；傳授審明，而迫奪之禍無有也。洞開諸門而悟君心之當正，蓋有契乎正心之學；偶讀《二典》而嘆法網之太密，蓋有得乎敬刑之旨。然宋之大綱固無愧於三代，而宋之法制則不迨於漢、唐。以詩賦記誦求士，而無學校養成之法；以科名資歷叙位，而無官司課試之方。選宿衛則不能變五代姑息羈縻之俗，教宗室則無以合先王親疎隆殺之宜。國用常病於空虛，兵威常患於不振，萬目未盡舉者，亦以誠之有未至也。漢、宋大綱雖云正矣，然因寵
translation_en:
… upheld was that their sincerity had not yet reached perfection and was adulterated by the way of the hegemon.

Emperor Taizong of the Tang established the garrison militia (fubing) system so that farmers were spared the expense of supporting troops; he instituted the law of hereditary land allotments (shiye) so that those below suffered no distress from land annexation; he employed the people through the grain-and-corvée (zuyong) tax system so that farmers had fixed livelihoods; and he appointed officials according to functional duties (zhishi) so that offices were not mere empty titles. His upholding of the myriad details of governance is deeply commendable. Yet by coercing his father to raise troops, the righteous bond between ruler and subject was estranged; by pressuring his father to abdicate the throne, the way of father and son was made deficient; by treading in blood at the palace gate, fraternal affection was thinned; and by herding like deer in the rear palace, the moral relation of husband and wife was thrown into disorder. Bestowing noble royal princesses in marriage upon chieftains of barbarian tribes meant that marital matches were improperly paired; and descending from the dignity of the Son of Heaven to assume [?] the title of Qaghan meant that there was no distinction between Chinese and barbarian. Therefore, as his descendants succeeded one another, their shameful conduct was manifold, and the great fundamental principles were never rectified. The reason they were not rectified was that his sincerity was not yet cultivated and was adulterated by barbarian ways.

When the Song founder laid the dynastic foundation, he established the state upon benevolence and righteousness. His obeying his mother'sloving instructions and not violating the covenant of the Golden Coffer displays his filial piety; his loving the Prince of Jin and ultimately entrusting him with the weighty sacred vessel of the throne displays his fraternal devotion. Family regulations were upright, and scandals within the palace women's quarters went unheard of; the transmission of the throne was clear and deliberate, and calamities of forced usurpation did not exist. Throwing open all the palace gates and realizing that the ruler's mind ought to be upright, he indeed had an affinity with the learning of rectifying the mind; happening to read the Two Canons (Erdian) of the Book of Documents and sighing that the net of the law was too dense, he indeed grasped the purport of reverent caution in punishments. Yet while the great fundamental principles of the Song truly had nothing to be ashamed of before the Three Dynasties, the institutional regulations of the Song did not match those of the Han and Tang. They sought scholars through poetry, rhapsodies, and rote memorization, lacking a method for nurturing talent in schools; they ranked official positions by examination degree and seniority, lacking a means for government agencies to evaluate performance. In selecting the palace guards, they could not transform the Five Dynasties' custom of indulgent appeasement and loose rein; in instructing the imperial clan, they had no way to accord with the former kings' standard of graduating honors according to closeness of kinship. State finances chronically suffered from depletion, and military might was chronically afflicted by weakness; that the myriad details were not fully upheld was likewise because their sincerity had not yet reached perfection.

Although the great fundamental principles of the Han and Song may be called upright, because of favoritism…

punctuated: 而啓人彘之禍，因爭而有廢后之失，其大綱亦豈盡正乎？唐之萬目雖云舉矣，然禮樂議而不能興，封建講而不能行，其萬目亦豈盡舉乎？洪惟我太祖高皇帝，勇智之資克配乎成湯，寛仁之度逺過於漢祖。取土宇於群盜攘斂之際，復人紀于胡元昏楺之餘。追帝先世，則武王尊親之孝也；封建諸王，則帝堯睦族之仁也。立學校以明人倫，正祀典以絶誣妄，后妃不得與政，戚畹不得秉權，其大綱正矣。置屯設守，則内外相承；列爵建官，則體統不紊。律令有定條，而人易於遵守；田賦有定制，而民易於轉輸。朝覲會同之禮，粲粲乎成周之大典；黜陟考課之法，鑿鑿乎隆古之弘規，其萬目舉矣。然其所以正大綱、舉萬目者，無非本於誠而已。繼是以來，太宗文皇帝、仁宗昭皇帝以是誠而出治，茂衍乎洪圖；宣宗章皇帝、英宗睿皇帝以是誠而守文，丕承乎駿烈。所以超漢、唐，軼有宋，而追踪於唐、虞、三代者，庸有出於此乎？仰惟陛下即位以來，隆大孝於兩宮，篤至仁於九族，御
translation_en:
… invited the calamity of the "human swine" [under Empress Lü], and because of a dispute [Song Renzong] committed the error of deposing the Empress; how then could their overarching principles be considered completely rectified? Although it is said that in the Tang dynasty the myriad particulars were all attended to, rites and music were discussed yet could not be revived, and enfeoffment was debated yet could not be put into practice; how then could its myriad particulars be considered completely attended to?

I reflect with awe upon our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu): his endowment of courage and wisdom was a worthy match for Cheng Tang, and his magnanimous and benevolent capacity far surpassed that of the Han Progenitor (Han Gaozu). He wrested the realm's territory amid the pillaging and extortion of bands of brigands, and restored human moral order in the aftermath of the benighted confusion of the barbarian Yuan. In posthumously elevating his ancestors to imperial rank, he showed the filial piety of King Wu in honoring his forebears; in enfeoffing the imperial princes, he displayed the benevolence of Emperor Yao in harmonizing the clan. He established schools to clarify human relationships, rectified the sacrificial statutes to put an end to delusive falsehoods, forbade empresses and imperial consorts from participating in governance, and prevented imperial relatives by marriage from wielding power—thus the overarching principles were rectified. In establishing military colonies and setting up garrisons, the interior and exterior supported one another; in ranking nobility and instituting offices, the hierarchical system was free of disorder. Laws and ordinances had fixed articles so that people could easily abide by them; land taxes had fixed regulations so that the commoners could easily transport and deliver them. The rites of court audiences and royal assemblies shone brilliantly like the grand canons of the flourishing Zhou; the methods of demotion, promotion, and personnel evaluation were as clear and definite as the vast designs of high antiquity—thus the myriad particulars were attended to. Yet the means by which he rectified the overarching principles and attended to the myriad particulars was nothing other than being rooted in sincerity.

In succession thereafter, Grand Ancestor Emperor Wen (Taizong) and Benevolent Ancestor Emperor Zhao (Renzong) brought forth governance through this sincerity, richly expanding the great plan; Proclaiming Ancestor Emperor Zhang (Xuanzong) and Eminent Ancestor Emperor Rui (Yingzong) maintained the civil order through this sincerity, grandly carrying on the illustrious achievements. How could that by which they surpassed Han and Tang, excelled Song, and followed in the footsteps of Tang [Yao], Yu [Shun], and the Three Dynasties go beyond this? Looking up in reflection since Your Majesty ascended the throne: you have exalted great filial piety toward the Two Palaces [the Empresses Dowager], deepened utmost benevolence toward the nine grades of kinsmen, attended…

聖學親政務以延攬英才大綱□有不正萬目寧有不舉

陛下幸太學以重儒道則人倫宜無不明矣教化所以厚
風俗也

下寬租之
令頻發內帑而施賑貸之恩宜乎百姓富庶而無失所

陛下之誠有未盡歟臣請為

官而食廪縻祿坐待他遷雖有司教之職而倖進苟
就無復自振以致為士者視合汙為常情詆好脩為

以清其本嚴考郡縣之貢以塞其流大掃夙昔之因

translation_en:
…the Classics Colloquium to continually illuminate Your sagely learning, and personally attend to state affairs to recruit and welcome outstanding talents. How could the great principles [?] not be rectified, and how could the myriad details not be attended to? Furthermore, the Confucian Way is that by which human relationships are clarified; since Your Majesty has visited the National University to honor the Confucian Way, human relationships ought to be entirely clarified. Moral transformation is that by which customs are enriched; since Your Majesty has established the August Ultimate to foster moral transformation, customs ought to be entirely enriched. You personally plowed the ceremonial field and issued orders to remit taxes, and frequently disbursed funds from the Inner Treasury to bestow the grace of famine relief and loans; it ought to be that the common people are prosperous and numerous, without the worry of losing their livelihoods. You practice military arts and train soldiers, repeatedly issuing edicts calling for vigilance and readiness, and dispatch armies and appoint generals, striving to achieve the merit of triumphant return; it ought to be that the four surrounding non-Chinese peoples submit in allegiance, without the trouble of obstructing civilization. Yet human relationships are not yet completely clarified, customs are not yet [completely] enriched, the common people still suffer the misery of crying out in hunger and wailing in the cold, and with the four surrounding non-Chinese peoples there is still the anxiety of them tyrannizing and doing violence to the weak. Could it be that Your Majesty's sincerity is not yet fully realized? Your servant begs to speak of this for Your Majesty.
That human relationships are not clarified is due to the neglect and laxity of educational administration. Today, although there are officials who supervise education, they consume grain stipends and waste salaries, sitting idly while waiting for transfer elsewhere; although there are posts in charge of instruction, their holders advance through lucky chance and take up office perfunctorily, no longer rousing themselves. As a result, scholars regard joining in corruption as normal sentiment, and slander fondness for self-cultivation as fishing for praise, while the empire is at a loss and does not know that the Confucian Way should be followed. If Your Majesty can truly entrust scholars of upright conduct and proper speech with the responsibility of revitalizing schools, carefully select students of the National University to purify the source, strictly examine tribute students from the prefectures and counties to stem the corrupt flow, sweep away the long-standing inertia of the past, and clearly show the empire the direction to pursue, then people will know shame and love righteousness, and how could human relationships…

来者進用而無書抵政府者或至於擯斥左右先容
者登庸而同巷不求見者或至于罷歸以致士夫之
間正色自持者見疎而諛言取悅者得志天下靡然

人而勿事姑息嚴察外任之不職而勿事模稜杜僥
倖之門重奔競之罰則人將斂華就實而風俗焉有
不厚者哉民不可以不安而安之則係於守令也今
之守令非國學因仍之徒即銓曹陸次之士跡其平
===
時不遂之心而肆其今日可為之勢以巧取民財為
良圖以期會簿書為能事如是而求百姓無失所之
憂未之有也臣願

之制而勿限其職于資格著循良之績者特褒而犯
貪污之罪者連坐將見守令皆賢才而百姓不難于
富庶矣夷不可以不攘而攘之則係於將帥也今之
將帥非勳戚之貴寵即廕襲之子弟以科斂侵牟為

translation_en: …fail to be made clear? That customs are not generous stems from the habits of scholars not being upright. Thus, those who traffic in bribes are promoted and employed, while those who send no letters to the high ministers of state may even end up rejected; those who have the monarch's attendants speak on their behalf in advance are elevated to office, while those living in the same lane who do not seek an audience may even end up dismissed and sent home. Consequently, among scholar-officials, those who maintain a stern integrity are alienated, whereas those who curry favor with flattering words achieve their ambitions, and the whole empire is swept along without knowing that integrity and honor are to be valued. If Your Majesty can truly place upright, firm, and discerning men at the head of the Ministry of Personnel, carefully weed out the mediocre men awaiting appointment without indulging in leniency, strictly investigate derelict provincial officials without resorting to ambiguity, close the gates to undeserved fortune, and stiffen the penalties for opportunistic intriguing, then men will turn away from flashiness toward substance—and how could customs fail to become generous? The people cannot be left without peace, and bringing them peace depends upon the prefects and magistrates. The prefects and magistrates of today, if not routinized students from the National University, are scholars appointed by the Ministry of Personnel merely according to seniority [? 陸次]. Following up on the frustrated desires of their ordinary days, they give free rein to the power they can wield today, regarding the clever extraction of the people's wealth as a fine strategy, and treating the meeting of deadlines and the keeping of registers as the height of capability. To act like this and yet expect the common people to be free of the worry of losing their livelihoods—such a thing has never happened. Your servant wishes that Your Majesty would restore the method of recommending scholars in ten categories, and not leave that authority solely to the Ministry of Personnel; and institute the system of the eight handles for controlling officials, and not restrict their posts by seniority and qualifications. If those who achieve the merit of upright and benevolent administration are specially commended, and those who commit the crime of corruption are subject to joint liability, we shall soon see that the prefects and magistrates are all worthy talents, and it will not be difficult for the common people to become prosperous and numerous. The barbarians cannot be left unrepelled, and repelling them depends upon the generals and commanders. The generals and commanders of today, if not favored nobles among the meritorious and imperial relatives, are the sons and younger brothers who inherit office through the protection privilege. They treat levying exactions and fleecing their subordinates as their regular occupation, and regard military reviews and training as taboo. In times of leisure they use illicit connections to advance, and when affairs end in defeat their hereditary stipends still remain. To act like this and yet hope that the barbarians of the four quarters will pose no danger of obstructing civilization—such a thing has never happened. Your servant…

… wish Your Majesty: if a Confucian scholar is fit to be a general, then grant him military authority without being constrained by the fact that he is a Confucian scholar; if a common soldier from the ranks is fit to be a general, then entrust him with frontier command without being limited by the fact that he is from the ranks. Reward wherever there is merit, leaving no one out because they are distant or estranged; dismiss wherever there is guilt, allowing no one to escape by luck because they are relatives or nobles. Then we shall see that all military commanders are fine men, and it will not be difficult to bring the four barbarian peoples into submission.

Yet all of these several matters depend solely on the sincerity of Your Majesty's own mind. Now the investigation of things and the extension of knowledge are the means to illuminate this sincerity; making the intentions sincere, rectifying the mind, and cultivating the person are the means to embody this sincerity. Licentious music and alluring beauty are enough to dissipate this sincerity; your servant wishes Your Majesty to banish seductive sounds and sights and not draw near to them. Palaces of jasper and terraces of jade are enough to divert this sincerity; your servant wishes Your Majesty to halt construction projects and not build them. Galloping about in hunting and fowling is a deadly poison that confuses this sincerity; your servant wishes Your Majesty to guard against excursions and hunts. Rare birds and strange beasts are weeds that harm this sincerity; your servant wishes Your Majesty to be prudent in your tastes and preferences. As for loyal and forthright words, may Your Majesty not reject them because they go against your heart, for this is the means to preserve this sincerity; as for flattering and sycophantic talk, may Your Majesty not follow it because it accords with your wishes, lest it drive a wedge into this sincerity. Nourish it in emptiness and tranquility, preserve it amidst tumult and confusion; cultivate your person by this, and govern by this. Why worry then that the great fundamental principles will not be rectified? Why worry that the myriad particular details will not be put into effect? Thereby you will add glory to your ancestors and match the splendor of the former sages; within and beyond the realm, a spring breeze of supreme harmony will prevail, and the virtue of double brilliance and the power of great succession will reside not in Shun and King Wu, but in Your Majesty.

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
陛下正心以為國家之大本獨斷以收威福之大權而已
盖心者所以具衆理權者所以宰萬事心不正則流
於異端而此誠無所主權不收則移於近習而此誠
無所施故箕子曰惟辟作福惟辟作威惟辟玉食孔子曰天下
有道禮樂征伐自天子出臣願
陛下鑒往哲之言作将来之戒運獨化於陶鈞裁萬機於
乾斷則何求不得何願不遂四者之事亦豈足致廑于
聖慮哉然欲收威福之柄又在正一己之心故曾子曰心
正而后身脩家齊國治天下平孟子曰君正莫不正
臣願
===
陛下端厥心居以為化本勿為邪說之所揺勿為外誘之
所奪則形端表直源潔流清以正天下之大綱以舉
天下之萬目者寔基于此也可不謹哉是則誠之一
字固
聖學之始終而正心獨斷二者尤
聖治之切要此臣所以繁其辭而不殺為
陛下言之也臣學不足以稽古才不足以應變然所言必
本於道不敢肆為淺近之說所陳必切於事不敢過
為迂遠之談惟
陛下留聽而採納焉幸甚臣謹對

punctuated: 陛下正心以為國家之大本，獨斷以收威福之大權而已。盖心者，所以具衆理；權者，所以宰萬事。心不正則流於異端，而此誠無所主；權不收則移於近習，而此誠無所施。故箕子曰：「惟辟作福，惟辟作威，惟辟玉食。」孔子曰：「天下有道，禮樂征伐自天子出。」臣願陛下鑒往哲之言，作将来之戒，運獨化於陶鈞，裁萬機於乾斷，則何求不得？何願不遂？四者之事，亦豈足致廑于聖慮哉？然欲收威福之柄，又在正一己之心。故曾子曰：「心正而后身脩、家齊、國治、天下平。」孟子曰：「君正，莫不正。」臣願陛下端厥心居以為化本，勿為邪說之所揺，勿為外誘之所奪，則形端表直、源潔流清，以正天下之大綱，以舉天下之萬目者，寔基于此也，可不謹哉！是則誠之一字，固聖學之始終，而正心、獨斷二者，尤聖治之切要。此臣所以繁其辭而不殺，為陛下言之也。臣學不足以稽古，才不足以應變，然所言必本於道，不敢肆為淺近之說；所陳必切於事，不敢過為迂遠之談。惟陛下留聽而採納焉，幸甚。臣謹對。
translation_en:
… Your Majesty to rectify your mind so as to establish the great foundation of the state, and to exercise sole decision-making power so as to hold fast the great authority over punishments and rewards—nothing more. For the mind is that whereby all principles are encompassed, and authority is that whereby the myriad affairs are governed. If the mind is not rectified, it will drift into heterodoxy, and this sincerity will have nothing to preside over it; if authority is not held fast, it will shift to close favorites, and this sincerity will have nowhere to be applied. Therefore Jizi said: "Only the sovereign makes good fortune; only the sovereign makes terror; only the sovereign eats the precious food." Confucius said: "When the Way prevails in the world, rites, music, and punitive expeditions proceed from the Son of Heaven." Your servant wishes that Your Majesty take the words of former sages as a mirror and make of them a warning for the future, wielding sole transformative power upon the potter's wheel of creation and deciding the myriad affairs of state through sovereign judgment. Then what could be sought and not obtained? What wish could go unfulfilled? And how could those four matters suffice to trouble Your Sacred thoughts?

Yet if one wishes to hold fast the handle of punishments and rewards, it further lies in rectifying one's own mind. Thus Master Zeng (Zengzi) said: "When the mind is rectified, the personal life is cultivated, the family is regulated, the state is rightly governed, and the world is made peaceful." Mencius said: "When the ruler is correct, none will fail to be correct." Your servant wishes that Your Majesty make upright the dwelling of your mind as the foundation of moral transformation, neither shaken by perverse doctrines nor robbed by external temptations. Then when the form is upright, the shadow is straight, and when the source is pure, the stream is clear; rectifying the great guiding principles of the world and raising up the myriad particulars of the world truly rest upon this foundation. How could one not be cautious!

Thus the single word "sincerity" is indeed the beginning and end of Sacred learning, while rectifying the mind and exercising sole decision-making power are especially crucial essentials of Sacred governance. This is why your servant has elaborated his words without abridgment in speaking of them for Your Majesty. Your servant's learning is insufficient to examine antiquity, and his talent is insufficient to respond to changing circumstances. Yet what I have said is necessarily rooted in the Way, not daring to indulge in shallow and near-sighted theories; and what I have set forth necessarily touches directly upon practical affairs, not daring to go to excess in pedantic and impractical talk. It would be the greatest fortune if Your Majesty would lend your attention and adopt them. Your servant respectfully replies.

text:
臣陸簡
臣對臣聞聖人之君天下必思以盡天下之道而成
天下之治焉道者治之原治者道之著道與治相為
體用也故有其道者必能成其治而無其治者由不
能盡其道帝者以是道而帝王者以是道而王伯者
自雜於是道亡者自棄於是道者也大哉道乎原于
天而備于聖人之一身聖人思盡其道以成其治又
何莫而非奉乎天命之大而不違哉恭惟
皇帝陛下以天縱之聖居
天位之尊而於奉
===
天行道之始寤寐俊傑圖起事功欲正天下之大綱欲舉
天下之萬目而斟酌古今推求明效以下詢於微遠
之小臣是心何心哉蓋思以盡天下之道而成天下
之治也臣誠愚昧何足以知之然聞易坤之六三有
曰含章可貞以時發也曷敢效六四之括囊以取无
咎之譏哉臣聞是道也極于至大而無外入於至小
而無內語其大則為三綱五常之理凡所以根本乎
人心維持乎世教者如網之有綱也故曰大綱焉語
其小則為萬事萬物之理凡可以黼黻乎人情經緯
乎國體者如網之有目也故曰萬目焉天命聖人以

translation_en:
Your servant Lu Jian 陸簡.
Your servant replies: Your servant has heard that when a sage rules as sovereign over the world, he must seek to fulfill the Way of the world in order to accomplish the governance of the world. The Way is the source of governance, and governance is the manifestation of the Way; the Way and governance serve as substance and function to one another. Therefore, one who possesses this Way will surely be able to accomplish governance, whereas one who lacks such governance fails because he is unable to fulfill the Way. The Emperors of antiquity became Emperors through this Way, and the Kings of antiquity became Kings through this Way; the Hegemons adulterated this Way for themselves, and those who perished abandoned this Way for themselves. Great indeed is the Way! It originates in Heaven and is complete within the single person of the sage. When the sage seeks to fulfill the Way in order to accomplish governance, how could any part of it not be a matter of reverently upholding the greatness of the Mandate of Heaven without transgression? Reverently considering Your Majesty the Emperor: endowed with Heaven-bestowed sageliness and occupying the supreme position of the Heavenly Throne, at the very beginning of your upholding Heaven and putting the Way into practice, waking and sleeping you yearn for outstanding talents and plan to raise up achievements and enterprises. Wishing to rectify the great guiding ropes of the world and to lift up the myriad meshes of the world, you weigh antiquity and the present and investigate clear effects, condescending to inquire of minor servants from humble and distant places. What kind of mind is this mind? Truly, it seeks to fulfill the Way of the world and accomplish the governance of the world. Your servant is truly ignorant and benighted—how could he be sufficient to know of this? Yet I have heard that on the third Yin line of the Kun hexagram in the Book of Changes (Yi) it is said: "Containing brilliance, one may be steadfast: one brings it forth at the proper time." How would I dare imitate the "tying up the sack" of the fourth Yin line, only to incur the reproach of merely seeking to avoid blame! Your servant has heard that this Way reaches to the utmost greatness where nothing lies outside it, and penetrates to the utmost smallness where nothing lies within it. Speaking of its greatness, it is the principle of the Three Bonds and Five Constant Virtues—all that by which human minds are rooted and worldly moral teaching is maintained, just as a net has its main headrope; therefore it is called the "great guiding ropes." Speaking of its smallness, it is the principle of the myriad affairs and myriad things—all that by which human sentiments are adorned and the structure of the state is woven together, just as a net has its meshes; therefore it is called the "myriad meshes." title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
君天下者此也聖人奉天以治天下者此也故大綱
不正固不足以為治萬目不舉亦非盡善之道觀夫
九族既睦萬邦協和而允釐百工庶績咸熈則堯之
大綱萬目何如也五典慎徽四方風動而九官十二
牧得人六府三事允殖則舜之大綱萬目何如也故
堯之道光被四表舜之道重華協帝豈不由大綱正
而萬目舉也哉至於三代相因其道一致大禹之彜
倫攸敘典常率由有典有則貽厥子孫關石和鈞有
於王府大綱萬目之道備矣成湯之載纘禹服肇脩
人紀懋官懋賞公于用人三風十愆警于有位大綱
===
萬目之道詳矣文王之化行於關睢麟趾武王之化
成於會極歸極以至發政施仁脩舉廢墜建官有三
百六十之屬制禮有三千三百之條其綱無不正而
目無不舉也故禹之道敷于四海湯之道彰信兆民
文王之道光於四方武王之道永清四海又豈不由
大綱正而萬目舉也哉自是而後漢之高帝興仁義
之師而君臣之義明割偏私之寵而父子之天復盟
白馬而大封同姓致太牢以首祀先師其大綱庶乎
正矣然封建廢而不復學校弛而不脩制禮雜就乎
秦儀造律攟摭乎秦法而萬目之不舉何取焉況夫

百六十之屬制禮有三千三百之條其綱無不正而
目無不舉也故禹之道敷于四海湯之道彰信兆民
文王之道光於四方武王之道率清四海又豈不由
大綱正而萬目舉也哉自是而後漢之高帝興仁義
之師而君臣之義明割偏私之寵而父子之天復顯
白馬而大封同姓致太牢以首祀先師其大綱庶乎
正矣然封建廢而不復學校弛而不脩制禮雜就乎
叔孫通造律攈摭乎秦法而萬目之不舉何取焉況夫
punctuated: 君天下者，此也；聖人奉天以治天下者，此也。故大綱不正，固不足以為治；萬目不舉，亦非盡善之道。觀夫九族既睦，萬邦協和，而允釐百工，庶績咸熈，則堯之大綱萬目何如也！五典慎徽，四方風動，而九官十二牧得人，六府三事允殖，則舜之大綱萬目何如也！故堯之道光被四表，舜之道重華協帝，豈不由大綱正而萬目舉也哉！至於三代相因，其道一致。大禹之彜倫攸敘，典常率由，有典有則，貽厥子孫，關石和鈞，有於王府，大綱萬目之道備矣；成湯之載纘禹服，肇脩人紀，懋官懋賞，公于用人，三風十愆，警于有位，大綱萬目之道詳矣；文王之化行於《關睢》、《麟趾》，武王之化成於會極、歸極，以至發政施仁，脩舉廢墜，建官有三百六十之屬，制禮有三千三百之條，其綱無不正而目無不舉也。故禹之道敷于四海，湯之道彰信兆民，文王之道光於四方，武王之道永清四海，又豈不由大綱正而萬目舉也哉！自是而後，漢之高帝興仁義之師，而君臣之義明；割偏私之寵，而父子之天復；盟白馬而大封同姓，致太牢以首祀先師，其大綱庶乎正矣。然封建廢而不復，學校弛而不脩，制禮雜就乎秦儀，造律攟摭乎秦法，而萬目之不舉，何取焉！況夫
translation_en:
… rule as sovereign over all under Heaven is precisely this, and that by which the sage obeys Heaven to govern all under Heaven is precisely this. Therefore, if the great headrope is not rectified, it is certainly insufficient to bring about good governance; and if the ten thousand meshes are not lifted into place, neither is it the Way of complete perfection.

Observe how when the nine branches of the clan had become harmonious and the ten thousand states were brought into concord, the hundred officials were truly regulated and all achievements were resplendent—how magnificent were the great headrope and the ten thousand meshes under Yao! When the Five Teachings were carefully beautified and the four quarters were moved as by the wind, the Nine Offices and Twelve Pastors obtained the right men, and the Six Treasuries and Three Affairs truly flourished—how magnificent were the great headrope and the ten thousand meshes under Shun! Thus the Way of Yao radiated across the four extremities, and the Way of Shun in doubled brilliance matched the former Emperor; was this not because the great headrope was rectified and the ten thousand meshes were lifted into place?

When it came to the Three Dynasties, which succeeded one another, their Way was identical. With Great Yu, the invariable human relationships were set in order, the constant norms were followed, statutes and rules were bequeathed to his descendants, and standard weights of stone and jun were kept in the royal treasury—thus the Way of the great headrope and the ten thousand meshes was complete. With Cheng Tang, he continued the旧 domain of Yu, initiated the cultivation of human moral bonds, rewarded official service and merit with impartiality in employing men, and warned those in office against the three decadent customs and ten faults—thus the Way of the great headrope and the ten thousand meshes was detailed. The transforming influence of King Wen operated through the Odes "Guanju" (Ospreys Cry) and "Linzhi" (Footsteps of the Unicorn), and the transforming influence of King Wu was completed in the convergence upon and return to the Supreme Ultimate; extending even to issuing governmental measures and practicing benevolence, restoring what had fallen into neglect, establishing offices with three hundred and sixty subordinates, and formulating rites with three thousand three hundred articles—there was no headrope not rectified and no mesh not lifted into place. Therefore the Way of Yu spread throughout the four seas, the Way of Tang manifested trustworthiness to the millions of people, the Way of King Wen shone across the four quarters, and the Way of King Wu forever purified the four seas; again, was this not because the great headrope was rectified and the ten thousand meshes were lifted into place?

From this time onward, Emperor Gao of Han raised an army of benevolence and righteousness so that the duty between ruler and minister was made clear; he severed his partial and private favor so that the natural bond between father and son was restored; he swore the white-horse covenant to grandly enfeoff those of the same surname, and offered the tailao sacrifice to be the first to worship the Former Teacher [Confucius]—his great headrope was nearly rectified. Yet the feudal system was abandoned and not restored, schools fell into laxity and were not repaired, the formulation of rites was promiscuously adapted from Qin ceremonies, and the making of statutes was gleaned from Qin laws; since the ten thousand meshes were not lifted into place, what was there to commend? Moreover,…

title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
分羹之語偽遊之擒倡始和親之謀養成吕氏之權
皆非所以示後世之道則其大綱亦未盡正也此其
治之所以不純者豈非其自雜於是道乎唐之太宗
力行仁義身致太平法周典以建官立府衛以置兵
役民有租庸調之法立政有律令格式之條其萬目
庶乎舉矣然好尚功名不及禮樂兄弟有推刃之殘
閨門有穢簿之恥承乾之變生藩籬垂拱之穢流衽
席胡雛一呼冠屨倒置叛臣屢作堂陛陵夷大綱之
不正何取焉况夫功德之舞變而為鄭衛之音府衛
之兵壞而為節度之制建官過於重複邊備失於疎
===
虞萬目亦未為盡舉也此其治之所以不正者豈非
其自棄于是道乎至如宋之太祖金匱一盟而母子
兄弟之道俱盡杯酒一言而君臣勲戚之義兩全閨
門著雍穆之風父子倡揖遜之美大綱之正豈不遠
過于漢唐之虛文哉奈何開國之初武畧不競國勢
浸衰天下之事似乎萎靡不治朝廷之制幾于廢弛
不舉惠褒而威失振賞數而加無功萬目之不舉終
不底夫唐虞三代之盛治焉况夫黃袍加身有慚北
面之義柱斧戳地卒啓後世之疑未幾太宗盟渝于
金匱天聖事出於簾帷大綱之不能盡正君子惜之

不正何取焉况夫功德之舞變而爲鄭衛之音府衛

===
虞萬目亦未爲盡舉也此其治之所以不正者豈非
其自棄于是道乎至如宋之太祖金匱一盟而母子
兄弟之道俱盡杯酒一言而君臣勲戚之義兩全閨
門著雍穆之風父子倡揖遜之美大綱之正豈不遠
過于漢唐之虛文哉奈何開國之初武畧不競國勢
浸衰天下之事似乎萎靡不治朝廷之制幾于廢弛
不舉恩褒而威失振賞數而加無功萬目之不舉終
不底夫唐虞三代之盛治焉况夫黃袍加身有慚北
面之義柱斧蝕地卒啓後世之疑未幾太宗盟渝于
金匱天聖事出于丁秦帷大綱之不能盡正君子惜之
punctuated: 分羹之語，偽遊之擒，倡始和親之謀，養成吕氏之權，皆非所以示後世之道，則其大綱亦未盡正也。此其治之所以不純者，豈非其自雜於是道乎？唐之太宗力行仁義，身致太平，法周典以建官，立府衛以置兵，役民有租庸調之法，立政有律令格式之條，其萬目庶乎舉矣。然好尚功名，不及禮樂；兄弟有推刃之殘，閨門有穢簿之恥；承乾之變生藩籬，垂拱之穢流衽席；胡雛一呼，冠屨倒置；叛臣屢作，堂陛陵夷。大綱之不正，何取焉？况夫功德之舞，變而為鄭衛之音；府衛之兵，壞而為節度之制；建官過於重複，邊備失於疎虞，萬目亦未為盡舉也。此其治之所以不正者，豈非其自棄于是道乎？至如宋之太祖，金匱一盟，而母子兄弟之道俱盡；杯酒一言，而君臣勲戚之義兩全。閨門著雍穆之風，父子倡揖遜之美，大綱之正，豈不遠過于漢唐之虛文哉？奈何開國之初，武畧不競，國勢浸衰；天下之事，似乎萎靡不治，朝廷之制，幾于廢弛不舉。惠褒而威失振，賞數而加無功，萬目之不舉，終不底夫唐、虞、三代之盛治焉。况夫黃袍加身，有慚北面之義；柱斧戳地，卒啓後世之疑。未幾，太宗盟渝于金匱，天聖事出於簾帷，大綱之不能盡正，君子惜之。
translation_en:
…remark about "sharing a cup of soup," the capture accomplished through a feigned excursion, the initiation of the marriage-alliance policy with the nomads, and the fostering of the Lü clan's power—none of these were ways to set an example for posterity, so his fundamental principles were not entirely rectified either. Why was his governance impure, if not because he himself adulterated this Way?

Emperor Taizong of the Tang vigorously practiced benevolence and righteousness and personally brought about great peace. He modeled his bureaucracy on the institutions of the Zhou, established the garrison militia (fuwei) to deploy troops, instituted the three-part tax system (zuyongdiao) in exacting service from the people, and set up the articles of statutes, ordinances, regulations, anditched ordinances (lüling geshi) in administering the government; thus his myriad details of administration were nearly all attended to. Yet he prized worldly achievement and fame and failed to reach the level of rites and music. Among brothers there was the brutality of fratricidal blades; within the inner quarters there was the shame of a sullied register. The rebellion of Li Chengqian arose within his own protective fence, and the debauchery of the Chuigong era (under Empress Wu) flowed from the bedchamber. At a single cry from the barbarian fledgling (An Lushan), cap and shoes were inverted; rebellious subjects repeatedly arose, and the dignity of the imperial court was eroded. When the fundamental principles are not rectified, what is there to commend? Moreover, the dances celebrating merit and virtue degenerated into the decadent airs of Zheng and Wei; the garrison militia decayed into the system of Military Commissioners (jiedushi); the bureaucracy became overly redundant; and border defenses suffered from carelessness and neglect—so the myriad details of administration were not entirely attended to either. Why was his governance unrectified, if not because he himself abandoned this Way?

As for Emperor Taizu of the Song, with the single covenant of the golden casket, the moral obligations between mother and son and between elder and younger brother were both fulfilled; with a single word over a cup of wine, the righteous duty between ruler and minister and toward meritorious relatives was preserved on both sides. The inner quarters displayed an air of harmonious solemnity, and father and son set an example of the beauty of courteous deference. In the rectification of fundamental principles, did he not far surpass the empty formalities of the Han and Tang? Yet why was it that at the founding of the dynasty, military strategy was uncompetitive and national power gradually waned; the affairs of the empire seemed listless and uncurbed, and the institutions of the court were almost lax and unattended to? Kindness was praised while awe failed to be roused; rewards were frequent and bestowed upon the meritless. Because the myriad details of administration were not attended to, in the end it failed to reach the flourishing governance of Tang (Yao), Yu (Shun), and the Three Dynasties. Moreover, having the yellow robe draped over his body left him ashamed before the righteous duty of a subject facing north; and the striking of the ground with the jade-headed axe ultimately aroused the suspicions of later generations. Before long, Emperor Taizong betrayed the covenant of the golden casket, and during the Tiansheng era (1023–1032) state affairs issued from behind ascreened curtain. That the fundamental principles could not be entirely rectified is something gentlemen regret.…

故宋室之治上不能優入乎帝王之域下不能屏迹
乎夷伯之途其為道也止於宋耳若我
太祖高皇帝為順天應人之舉成用夏變夷之功得天下

大誥三編無非匡翼振德之言其規模宏遠矣大綱之正
有一不如唐虞三代乎至于內設六卿以總治天下
外設三司以分理萬邦其制兵深得夫統馭之方其
取民不出乎什一之法下至宮廬服食皆有數度車
===
書器用皆有法程其制作周密矣萬目之舉有一不
如唐虞三代者乎此之謂大哉聖人之道洋洋乎發
育萬物峻極于天道無大而不行優優大哉禮儀三
百威儀三千道無小而不備以德則帝以功則王而
一洗千古雜夷雜伯之陋也至於
列聖相承所以盡其道成其治以奉乎
天者益久而益隆故天下百年來國無異政家無殊俗四
方上下無不治安猶倚南山以坐平原也然臣竊聞
之天道三月一小變先王之道亦有偏而不起之處

translation_en:
Therefore, in the governance of the Song royal house, above it could not enter generously into the realm of the Five Emperors and Three Kings, and below it could not banish all traces of the paths of barbarians and hegemons; its Way stopped at being merely that of the Song.

As for our Grand Progenitor, Emperor Gao (Taizu Gaohuangdi), he undertook actions that complied with Heaven and responded to men, and accomplished the achievement of using Chinese ways to transform the barbarians. In gaining the empire, he had none of the shameful failings of the Tang and Song; in governing the empire, he possessed the far-sighted plans of Yu and Zhou. He posthumously enfeoffed Ancestor Ren (Renzu), putting filial piety first before the myriad people; he enfeoffed the Imperial Princes, using grace to encourage those of the same surname. The single book of the Ancestral Injunctions (Zuxun) is nothing other than the learning of subtlety, unity, and holding fast to the Mean; the three parts of the Grand Pronouncements (Dagao) are nothing other than words of rectification, assistance, and rousing virtue. His framework was vast and far-reaching indeed! In the rectitude of the great principles, was there a single thing inferior to Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties? As for establishing the Six Ministers within the court to exercise general governance over the empire, and establishing the Three Offices in the provinces to separately administer the myriad regions; his system for the military deeply grasped the method of command and control, and his exactions from the people did not go beyond the law of the one-tenth tithe; down to dwellings, clothing, and food, all had their prescribed numbers and measures, and carriages, writing, and implements for use, all had their standards and regulations. His institutions and creations were comprehensive and meticulous indeed! In the maintenance of the myriad details, was there a single thing inferior to Tang, Yu, and the Three Dynasties? This is what is meant by: "Great is the Way of the Sage! Overflowing, it brings forth and nourishes all things and rises up to the height of Heaven"—there is nothing in the Way so great that it is not put into practice; and "All-complete and great! Three hundred rules of ceremony, and three thousand rules of demeanor"—there is nothing in the Way so small that it is not provided for. By virtue he was an Emperor, by merit he was a King, washing away at once the vulgarity of a thousand ages that mixed in barbarian and hegemonic ways.

Coming down to the successive sacred emperors who inherited the throne, that by which they fulfilled their Way and perfected their governance so as to serve Heaven has grown ever more enduring and ever more flourishing. Therefore, for a hundred years across the empire, the state has had no divergent policies and families have had no differing customs; in all four quarters, above and below, there is nowhere that is not at peace and well-governed, just like leaning against the Southern Mountains while sitting upon a level plain. Yet your servant has privately heard it said that the Way of Heaven undergoes a minor change every three months, and even in the Way of the former kings there were places where it leaned to one side and failed to rise up. title: 成化二年進士登科錄
text:
孝弟之風或衰禮義之維或缺人倫其可不明乎然
人倫未明道未明也道既明於
陛下則民得於觀感興起之餘者秉彝好德自莫不復其
初矣庶政之脩風俗為始察於四民之內而巧偽之
弊日甚廉恥之風日微風俗其可不厚乎然風俗未
厚道未厚也道既厚於
陛下則民居於甄陶鼓舞之下者興仁興讓自莫不從其
好矣人倫既明風俗既厚則大綱不外是而正也至
如安國家保社稷者百姓也
陛下誠見夫民乏兼日之食廩無半歲之儲吾民之失所
===
可憂也然書曰德惟善政政在養民是養之有其道
耳
陛下能盡此道而明信法令平易刑賞年豐則安養之力
愈至年飢則救恤之惠弘敷使其養生送死之無憾
又何失所之可憂哉至於奉職貢効勤誠者四夷也
陛下誠見夫胡羌俟隙於西北蠻虜跳梁於東南遠人之
梗化可患也然傳曰懷遠以德立德以威是懷之有
其道耳
陛下能盡此道而君臣同德法度昭明使兵食既足邊圉
自固則彼畏威懷德之不暇又何梗化之足患哉百

punctuated: 孝弟之風或衰，禮義之維或缺，人倫其可不明乎？然人倫未明，道未明也；道既明於陛下，則民得於觀感興起之餘者，秉彝好德，自莫不復其初矣。庶政之脩，風俗為始；察於四民之內，而巧偽之弊日甚，廉恥之風日微，風俗其可不厚乎？然風俗未厚，道未厚也；道既厚於陛下，則民居於甄陶鼓舞之下者，興仁興讓，自莫不從其好矣。人倫既明，風俗既厚，則大綱不外是而正也。至如安國家、保社稷者，百姓也。陛下誠見夫民乏兼日之食，廩無半歲之儲，吾民之失所可憂也。然《書》曰：「德惟善政，政在養民。」是養之有其道耳。陛下能盡此道，而明信法令，平易刑賞，年豐則安養之力愈至，年飢則救恤之惠弘敷，使其養生送死之無憾，又何失所之可憂哉？至於奉職貢、効勤誠者，四夷也。陛下誠見夫胡羌俟隙於西北，蠻虜跳梁於東南，遠人之梗化可患也。然《傳》曰：「懷遠以德，立德以威。」是懷之有其道耳。陛下能盡此道，而君臣同德，法度昭明，使兵食既足，邊圉自固，則彼畏威懷德之不暇，又何梗化之足患哉？百

Yet if human relationships are not yet clarified, it is because the Way is not yet clarified; once the Way is clarified by Your Majesty, then the people, inspired and aroused by observing your example, holding fast to their innate constancy and loving virtue, will naturally all return to their original goodness. In the cultivation of the myriad affairs of governance, customs come first. Looking among the four classes of people, the abuses of artful deceit grow worse by the day, and the ethos of integrity and a sense of shame dwindles daily—how then can customs not be made generous and thick? Yet if customs are not yet generous, it is because the Way is not yet generous; once the Way is made generous by Your Majesty, then the people, living under your molding and encouraging influence, rising up in benevolence and rising up in yielding courtesy, will naturally all follow what you love. Once human relationships are clarified and customs are made generous, the overarching principles of governance will be rectified through nothing other than this. As for those who bring peace to the state and preserve the altars of soil and grain, they are the common people. Your Majesty truly sees that the people lack food for two days together and the granaries hold not half a year's stores, so that our people's loss of livelihood is cause for worry. Yet the Book of Documents (Shu) says: "Virtue is seen in good government, and government is tested by the nourishing of the people." This means that nourishing them has its proper Way. If Your Majesty can fulfill this Way—making laws and ordinances clear and trustworthy, making punishments and rewards fair and mild, redoubling efforts to bring peace and nourishment in years of plenty, and broadly extending the grace of relief and succor in years of famine, so that they have no regrets in nourishing the living or burying the dead—then what worry could there be over their losing their livelihood? As for those who present tribute and offer diligent allegiance, they are the four barbarian peoples. Your Majesty truly sees that the northern and western nomads (Hu and Qiang) watch for openings in the northwest, while the southern and northern tribes (Man and Lu) leap about rebelliously in the southeast, so that the obstinate resistance to transformation by distant peoples is cause for concern. Yet the Commentary (Zhuan) says: "Cherish the distant through virtue; establish virtue through awe-inspiring might." This means that cherishing them has its proper Way. If Your Majesty can fulfill this Way—with ruler and ministers united in virtue and laws and institutions brilliantly clear, ensuring that troops and provisions are sufficient and the frontier defenses are naturally secure—then they will be fully occupied with fearing your might and cherishing your virtue; what concern could there be over their obstinate resistance to transformation? 而無道無一物而非
陛下所有則無一物不有道以治之詩曰天降厥士曰監

聰明天明威自我民明威而民則道與治之所及也
陛下欲盡其道以成其治又可不知所以奉乎天而不忽

矣然臣願

…[harmonize] rites and music [?], enrich the Four Seas, and bring substance to the Four Barbarian Peoples, then all the myriad details can be attended to without toil. Once the great guiding principles are rectified and the myriad details are attended to, even though the realm is vast, all of it without exception will be encompassed within Your Majesty's moral transformation. Then Your achievements will shed glory as successor to the One Progenitor and Four Ancestors, and Your virtue will continue the transmission of the Two Emperors and Three Kings; compared to this, how could the pettiness of the Han, Tang, and Song even be worth mentioning!

Even so, in all the realm there is not a single thing that was not born of Heaven, and thus not a single thing without its Way; and there is not a single thing that does not belong to Your Majesty, and thus not a single thing that does not have a Way by which it should be governed. The Classic of Poetry (Shi) says: "Heaven sends down its gentlemen [?], and its oversight is right here." And scholars are where the Way and governance reside. The Classic of Documents (Shu) says: "Heaven's hearing and seeing come through our people's hearing and seeing; Heaven's discernible awe comes through our people's discernible awe." And the common people are those whom the Way and governance reach. If Your Majesty wishes to fulfill this Way in order to accomplish this governance, how could You not know how to revere Heaven without neglect?

Moreover, as for that by which Heaven is Heaven: the unitary primal vital force never ceases and the four seasons proceed thereby—this is the rectification of the great guiding principles; the movements of the Five Phases complement one another and the hundred things are born thereby—this is the attending to the myriad details. If Your Majesty truly stands in reverent communion with Heaven when walking alone in the deep palace, and embodies this in practice when weighing and deciding affairs in the great court—wishing Your capacity to be as vast as Heaven's, Your action to be as vigorous as Heaven's, Your lofty brilliance to be like the shining down of the sun and moon, and Your awe-inspiring trustworthiness to be like the striking of thunder and lightning; extending and carrying forward the rectification of the great guiding principles until Heaven and Earth are established in their proper places, and expanding and filling out the attending to the myriad details until birds, beasts, grasses, and trees all flourish according to their natures—then human hearts will be harmonious below, the Way of Heaven will respond above, and Your Majesty will regulate and assist the course of nature in their midst. translation_en: … Could the means by which Your Majesty serves Heaven be sought in the midst of emptiness and non-being, or in some dark and unfathomable realm? Indeed, one who speaks well of Heaven must verify it in human affairs; and as this Way exists among men, the worthy understand its greater aspects while the unworthy understand its lesser ones. The Book of Documents (Shu) says: "He who likes to ask becomes abundant; he who relies only on himself becomes small." It also says: "When wood follows the ink-line, it becomes straight; when the sovereign follows remonstrance, he becomes sage." With the solitary person of a single body, Your Majesty is entrusted with ten thousand affairs of state; dwelling deep within the ninefold palace enclosures, You govern all within the four seas—how could You not clarify Your vision and extend Your hearing so as to draw broadly upon others? Therefore, what your servant wishes Your Majesty to seek from others consists of two things. The first is the Classics Colloquium (jingyan), by which to seek how our governance is rooted in the Way. Your Majesty indeed already attends the Classics Colloquium daily to expound and seek out the ultimate principles; yet You must advance day by day and progress month by month, continuing and brightening Your learning toward illumination like King Cheng, and not merely displaying it for fine appearance. The second is accepting remonstrance, by which to seek how our Way is manifested in governance. Your Majesty indeed already first sent down gracious decrees to throw open the avenues of speech; yet You must delight in questioning and examining, drawing upon others to practice goodness like Shun of Yu, and not merely treating it as a secondary matter. Thus Your sagely mind will be luminous and greatly enlightened, and Your sagely virtue will be pure, unified, and unadulterated; Your will shall find peace in the Way, and Your words shall be received according to the Way. Knowing that impartiality, rectitude, benevolence, and righteousness constitute the Way, You will know that artful evil and indulgent desires are not our Way, and will surely ponder how to keep them at a distance. Knowing that harmonious prosperity and supreme peace constitute good governance, You will know that perverse contention and noxious ills are not our governance, and will surely ponder how to eliminate them. punctuated: 大綱之當正、萬目之當舉為盡吾道之事，則知其未正未舉迺所以為害吾道之端；知盡其道、成其治者為所以奉乎天，則又豈有一念之非天哉！循是二者舉而行之，而不使怠惰之意少動于清衷，則陛下惓惓之心日謹一日，而功德所就沛然莫之能禦矣，又豈臣等所能測識其端倪哉！然臣聞之孟軻曰：「君子之事君也，務引其君以當道。」故敢舉此以為陛下獻。但臣愚，才有限而道無窮，心欲言而口不逮，不足以副陛下望道未見之誠，臣不勝畏罪之至。臣謹對。
translation_en: …that setting right the great guiding principles and raising up the myriad details of administration is the business of fulfilling our Way, then one knows that leaving them unrectified and unraised is the beginning of harm to our Way; and if one knows that fulfilling the Way and accomplishing good governance is the means by which to serve Heaven, then how could there be even a single thought that is not in accord with Heaven! If Your Majesty follows these two principles, raises them up and puts them into practice, without allowing the slightest thought of negligence or indolence to stir within Your pure mind, then Your Majesty's earnest devotion will grow more cautious day by day, and the achievements and virtue You accomplish will flow forth abundantly so that nothing can stem them—how could Your servants even fathom their bounds! Yet Your servant has heard that Meng Ke (Mencius) said: "When a gentleman serves his ruler, he strives to guide his ruler to keep to the proper Way." Therefore I have ventured to raise these points and present them to Your Majesty. However, Your servant is foolish: my talent is limited while the Way is inexhaustible, and though my heart wishes to speak, my mouth falls short, so that I am inadequate to match Your Majesty's sincerity in gazing toward the Way as though You had not yet seen it. Your servant is overcome with the utmost fear of giving offense. Your servant respectfully replies.
